pages.text: BDCPC301 - Use pre- intermediate English at the workplace Competence CCMEN302 RQF Level: 3 Learning Hours 30 Credits: 3 Sector: All Trade: All Module Type: Complementary Curriculum: All TVET Certificate 3 Copyright: © Rwanda TVET Board, 2023 Issue Date: May 2023 x 1200

1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This complementary module describes the skills, knowledge and attitudes to be acquired by level three learner according to RQF in order to communicate simply using English in familiar situations. The learner will be able to n arrate about familiar and social events and write short compositions on familiar topics. Learner also will be able to read and interpret messages from simple texts and then react to common trade- related oral English. `Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 100% Practical work: 70% 70% • Group work and presentation 40% • Individual Work and presentation 30% Summative Assessment N/A Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Narrate about familiar and social events 1.1. Social events are effectively described using descriptive words. 1.2. Social events attended are appropriately explained using WH- Questions. 1.3. Professional experiences and ambitions are properly summarized through debates and dialogues. 2. Write short compositions on familiar topics 2.1. Paragraph is correctly organised using building blocks of sentences. 2.2. Paragraph is effectively written using punctuation marks. 2.3. Paragraph is correctly developed based on its types. 3. Read and interpreting messages from simple texts 3.1. Specific information from the text read is precisely discovered based on types of reading. 3.2. The text is effectively comprehended based on the identification of the most important ideas in the text. 3.3. Lessons conveyed by the texts are effectively identified based on text purpose.

2 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 4. React to common trade-related oral English 4.1. Types and components of speech are effectively described based on the speech purpose. 4.2 Expressions on the recording listened to are properly expressed with own opinions/views. 4.3. Ideas and opinions raised in simple trade-related recording/ speeches are defended based on critical discussion. 4.4. Specific questions on a trade-related audio material are precisely answered using active listening.

3 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Course content Learning outcomes At the end of the module the learner will be able to: 1. Narrate about familiar events and activities. 2. Write short compositions on familiar topics. 3. Read and interpret messages from simple texts. and social letter. 4. React to common trade-related oral English. 1. Learning outcome 1: Narrate about familiar events and activities Learning hours: 7 Indicative content • Narration of familiar events using descriptive words ✓ Adjectives ✓ Adverbs ✓ Articles • Explanation of social activities using: ✓ WH- Questions. Who When Where What How Why ✓ Conjunctions Types of conjunctions Expressing of conjunctions • Discussion about professional experiences and ambition ✓ Dialogues Elements Rules ✓ Debates Structure Steps

4 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Resources required for the learning outcome Equipment White board, chalkboard, radio, projector, computer laptop Materials Markers, pieces of chalk, markers, flipcharts, pen, pieces of paper Tools Reference books,trainee manual Facilitation techniques Demonstration ,individual and group work, practical exercise ,group discussion Formative assessment methods Written assessment , Oral assessment Learning outcome 2: Write short compositions on familiar topics Learning hours: 8 Indicative content • The use of building blocks of sentences/ paragraph ✓ Types of sentence structure: simple sentence compound sentence complex sentence compound-complex sentence ✓ The building blocks of a simple sentence /clause Subject Predicate ✓ Complement/ Predicative noun/adjective ✓ Adverbial/prepositional phrases ✓ The building blocks of paragraph(Parts) Topic sentence Supporting sentences Concluding sentence

5 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation • The use of Punctuation marks ✓ Identify punctuations in sentences/ paragraph ✓ Use different punctuation marks in sentences, paragraphs and texts • Developing paragraph: ✓ Types of paragraph A descriptive paragraph A narrative paragraph An explanatory paragraph A persuasive paragraph ✓ Writing a well-structured paragraph Resources required for the indicative content Equipment White board, chalkboard, radio, projector, computer laptop Materials Markers, pieces of chalk, markers, flipcharts, pen, pieces of paper Tools Reference books, trainee manual Facilitation techniques Demonstration, individual and group work, practical exercise, trainer guided , group discussion Formative assessment methods Written assessment

6 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Learning outcome 3: Read and interpreting messages from simple texts and social letter Learning hours: 7 Indicative content • Getting specific information from the text. ✓ Types of reading Skimming Scanning Intensive Extensive • Depicting most important ideas in the text ✓ Main ideas ✓ Supporting ideas ✓ Detailed information ✓ Examples/ illustrations of ideas • Identification of the lessons conveyed by the text ✓ Text purpose Advising Warning Instructing Informing Resources required for the indicative content Equipment White board, chalkboard, radio and projector Materials Markers, pieces of chalk Tools Recordings, books, trainee manual Facilitation techniques Demonstration, individual and group work, practical exercise and group discussion Formative assessment methods Written assessment, oral presentation

7 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Learning outcome 4: React to common trade-related oral English. Learning hours: 8 Indicative content • Description of speech ✓ Definition of speech ✓ Kinds of speech according to the purpose Informative Speech that Persuasive Speech Entertains Speech Entertaining speech Motivational speech Impromptu speech Oratorical speech ✓ Effective speaking skills Definition of effective speaking Effective speaking strategies ✓ Components of speech Introduction The main point or body The conclusion Transitions ✓ Use of active listening to separate components of a speech Reporting of the main points of the speech/recording Keep an open mind ✓ Ways of reporting a speech To use exact words of the speaker To paraphrase what the speaker said To summarize the speech • Expressing own opinions / view ✓ Expression to be used for one’s own views In my view….. In my opionion….. Personally…. To be host….. To tell the truth…. According to…. As far as I am concerned/ is concerned….

8 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation From my point of view….. I agree/ disagree… I think that ….. I would like to…. • Critical discussion of ideas and opinions ✓ Sides/Positions of the discussions Supporting an idea Refuting/ rebutting an idea ✓ Using linkers/ connectors to defend one’s side First of all Last but not least On one hand On the other hand While, whereas For instance On the contrary As a result In addition to… • Answering to specific questions related to an audio material ✓ Use of active listening to understand an audio The main points Supporting details/ commentary Reporting the main points of the audio Resources required for the indicative content Equipment White board, chalkboard, flipchart, pen, pieces of paper. Materials Markers, pieces of chalk Tools Recording, reference, books, trainee manual, lesson plan, radio, projector Facilitation techniques Demonstration, individual and group work, practical exercise, group discussion Formative assessment methods Written assessment, oral asssement References: 1. Arnaudet, Martin L. and Mary Ellen Barrett. Paragraph Development : A Guide for Students of English. 2nd edition.

9 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 2. Buckley, J. The Canadian Student’s Guide to Essay Writing. (6th ed.) Toronto, 2004 3. Judith Humphrey, “Writing Professional Speeches,” Vital Speeches of the Day, vol. 54, Mar. 15, 1988, p. 343 4. Prof. Rosella Torrecampo Resource Person, “Basic Online Writing Training” iSchools Project Visayas State University, Babay, Leyte 5. Weissberg, Robert C. “Given and New : Paragraph Development Models from Scientific English.” TESOL Quarterly 18 (September 1984): 485-500.

x | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation FOREWORD The global rapid changes in the labour market tends do call for appropriate training and skills development through outcome-based training approaches. Skills development and employment promotion are central to Rwanda’s transformative Vi sion 2050, aiming to secure high standards of living for all Rwandans. In a bid to transform Rwanda into a knowledge based economy, the National Strategic Transformation 1(NST1) calls socio- economic transformation through TVET skills development. The Rwanda TVET Board (RTB) was established to promote quality education in technical and vocation education and training from level one (1) to five (5) aimed at fast tracking socio-economic development of the country. Designing and distributing curricula, teaching materials, trainer’s guides, methodologies and establish training methods for technical and vocation education and training from level one (1) to five (5); is among other RTB’s responsabilities . The existing curricula were limited and narrowed in terms of acquired skills and knowledge and were not meeting the requirements of the current labour market at both national and regional level. In addition there were. Barriers in vertical mobility and pathways in TVET which resulted in negative TVET perception. Furthermore, the were barriers to admission of TVET graduates of certain programs into higher learning institutions. The TVET modernization process has begun with a clear picture of the programs focusing on sector with the high employment potential like Land Surveying among others. In this respect, Rwanda TVET Board, in collaboration with ENABEL, is honoured to avail the revised curriculum of Land Surveying which serves as the official document and respond to the above mentioned concerns. With the help of the training providers, trainers, parents whose role is central to the success of this curriculum, the trainees will gain appropriate hand on skills which will make a difference not only to their own lives but also to the success of Rwanda’s economy. I wish to sincerely extend my appreciation to the people who contributed towards the development of this document. Eng._ Dip. Paul UMUKUNZI Director General/ RTB

1 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 1. GENERAL INTRODUCTION The curriculum presents a coherent and significant set of competencies to perform the occupation/s of a Building Set out Surveyor, Linear projects Surveyor and Surveyor’s Helper. It is designed with an approach that takes into account the training needs, the work situation, as well as the goals and the means to implement the training. The modules of the curriculum include a description of the expected results of the training. They have a direct influence on the choice of the theoretical and practical learning activities. The competencies are the targets of the training: the acquisition of each is required for certification. The curriculum is the reference to carry out the assessment of learning. Assessment tools of learning are developed based on this document. The curriculum consists of three parts. The first part is of general interest and shows the nature and goals of the program and the key concepts and definitions used in the document. The second part presents the qualification, its level in the qualification framework, its purpose, its rationale and the list of modules it comprises. The third part deals with the training package. It includes the competencies chart, the sequencing of module learning, the description of each module and the course structure. The pages describing the modules are the heart of a curriculum. They present the title of the module, the length of training, the amount of credits, the context in which the competency is performed, the prerequisite competencies, the learning units and the performance criteria. In each module, a course structure is provided. The course structure describes the learning outcomes (knowledge, skills and attitudes) and the learning contents related to each learning unit. In addition, the learning activities and resources for learning are included and where applicable, reference standards are mentioned for indicative contents. Standard reference numbers are indicated throughout the text and the full standards’titles in a separate list under reference section. Finally, the assessment specifications and guidelines are included in each module.

2 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 1.1. Rationale of the Qualification Rwanda’s building and construction industry has rapidly grown in the past couple of years with both government and private sector engaged in the construction of buildings, roads, dams, water treatment plants and new fresh water supply lines, and other infrastructures triggering what is now dubbed as a “construction boom in Rwanda”. The construction industry contributes immensely towards the GDP of the Country mainly through direct income and massive employment opportunities generated from various infrastructure projects, rehabilitation and maintenance. It is estimated that the construction sub-sector of the lar ger industrial sector contributes the highest to the country’s industrial GDP. However, there has been a shortage in skilled surveyors to work in the various formentioned constructions. As such skilled Surveyor worker is the key occupation that need to be addressed to drive the target of the government in construction sector.

ASSESSMENT GUIDELINES 4.1 Assessment Methodology To assess knowledge, practical, and application skills through a jury system of continuous evaluation that encourages learners to display understanding of the principles in application to set practical tasks and their attendant theory to assess self-learning. There are two types of assessment (Formative Assessment and Summative/Integrated Assessment). Each assessment has its own rule for passing to be declared competent. Formative Assessment This is applied on all types of modules (e.g. Complementary, General and Specific modules) A trainee to be competent for a formative module must have at least 70% A trainee to be eligible to undertake integrated assessment of specific modules must have at least 50% as passing line for general and complementary modules. Each trainee should be competent on all formative assessments to be declared competent on that module All formative assessment should be declared competent before taking the summative/integrated assessment

12 | P a g e Summative Assessment All Summative/Integrated assessment should match with the content of the module in the curriculum. Summative/Integrated Assessment is always in practical, giving it as a theoretical type of assessment is not acceptable. The integrated situation provided in the curriculum is a sample of the assessment to be carried out, the Trainer/Teacher has the role of developing another one referring to the task to be carried out in the integrated situation in accordance to the circumstances inside school, but the integrated situation should stick on the components of a task. During Summative/Integrated assessment, assessor panel members should be three (3). The trainee can be declared competent based on the assessment CRITERIA and its respective assessment indicators The Passing Line for the modules is: ▪ 50 % for general and complementary modules ▪ 70 % for specific modules Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 50% Practical work: 70% 70% Group project and presentation 20% Individual project /Work 50% Summative Assessment 50% Note: 1. Summative assessment is always conducted at the completion of module delivery. It should be practical through an integrated situation for specific modules and in any other forms of assessment for complementary and general modules. 2. Learing hours assigned to specific module includes the duration assigned to integrated assessment.

13 | P a g e GLOSSARY Assessment : A process of gathering and judging evidence in order to decide whether a person has attained a standard of performance. Assessment criteria: Statements which describe performances and place them in context with sufficient precision to allow valid and reliable assessment. Best practice: Management practices and work processes that lead to outstanding or top-class performance and provide examples for others. Competency standard: An industry- determined specification of performance which sets out the skills, knowledge and attitudes required to operate effectively in employment. Competency standards are made up of units of competency, which are themselves made up of elements of competency, together with performance criteria, a range of variables, and an evidence guide. Competency :means the ability to apply knowledge, skills and personal, social and methodological skills in the workplace or during learning, as well as in personal and professional development. This ability or capacity is acquired through leaning, exposure to the tasks and series of training allowing one to perform specific task autonomously. Reason why in the context of the CBE Framework competencies are described as responsibility and independence. Competency-based assessment (or CBA): The gathering and judging of evidence in order to decide whether a person has achieved a standard of competency. Complementary competencies: Set of knowledge, skills and attitudes which are not directly linked to a specific occupation or industry, but which are important for work, education and life in general, such as communication, mathematics, organizational aptitude, and computer literacy, interpersonal and analytical competency. Core modules: Modules leading to competencies’ acquisition that an indus try sector has agreed upon as essential for a person to be accepted as competent at a particular level. All modules may be core, but in many cases competency at a level will involve core modules plus optional or specialization modules. Core competencies are normally those central to work in a particular industry. Credential: Formal certification issued for successful achievement of a defined set of outcomes, e.g. successful completion of a course in recognition of having achieved particular knowledge, skills or competencies; successful completion of an apprenticeship or traineeship. Credit : The acknowledgement that a person has satisfied the requirements of a module. Curriculum: The specifications for a course or subject (module) which describe all the learning experiences a learner undergoes, generally including objectives, content, intended learning outcomes, teaching methodology, recommended or prescribed assessment tasks, assessment exemplars, etc. Evidence guide: The part of a competency standard which provides a guide to the interpretation and assessment of the unit of competency, including the aspects which need to be emphasized in assessment, relationships to other units,

14 | Page Skills for a better destiny and the required evidence of competency. Flexible delivery: A range of approaches to providing education and training, giving learners greater choice of when, where and how they learn. Flexible delivery may involve distance education, mixed-mode delivery, online education, self-paced learning, self-directed learning, etc. Formal education: Also formal training education or training provided in educational institutions such as schools, universities, colleges, etc. or off the job in a workplace, usually involving direction from a teacher or instructor. General competencies: competencies correspond to larger operations that go beyond the tasks, but generally contribute to their implementation. These activities require more fundamental learning and are generally common to several tasks and transferable to many work situations. Generic modules : Modules leading to the attainment of complementary competencies. Informal education: The acquisition of knowledge and skills through experience, reading, social contact, etc. Internship : An opportunity for a learner to integrate career related experience by participating in planned, supervised work. Key competencies: Any of several generic skills or competencies considered essential for people to participate effectively in the workforce. Key competencies apply to work generally, rather than being specific to work in a particular occupation or industry. The following are key areas of competency which were developed into seven key competencies: collecting, analyzing and organizing information; communicating ideas and information; planning and organizing activities; working with others and in teams; using mathematical ideas and techniques; solving problems; and using technology. Knowledge: means the result of the adoption of information through the learning process. Knowledge is a set of facts, principles, theories and practices related to area of work or study. In CBE context lifelong learning knowledge is described as theoretical and / or factual. Learning outcomes : are statements of what learner knows, understands and can perform, based on the completion of the learning process, defined by knowledge, skill and competency. Learning activities: Suggested activities that can be developed during lesson planning and activity preparation. The choice of learning activities must be tailored according to group size, available material resources and communication tools. Learning hours: Amount of hours required to acquire the competency, including the time allocated to evaluation, which is estimated between 5 and 10% of the total learning time of the competency. Learning outcomes: Statements that indicate what learners will know or be able to do as a result of a learning activity. Learning outcomes are usually expressed as knowledge, skills, or attitudes. Learning unit: Any of the basic building blocks of a module, which describes the key activities or the elements of the work covered by the module Module : A unit of training which corresponds to one competency and which can be completed on its own or linked to others. Occupation : The principal business of one’s life.

15 | Page Skills for a better destiny Performance criteria The part of a competency standard specifying the required level of performance in terms of a set of outcomes which need to be achieved in order to be deemed competent. It describes the quality requirements of the result obtained in labor performance. Qualification : means the formal name for the result of a process of assessment and validation, which is obtained when a competent body determines that an individual has achieved learning outcomes to the standards laid down. Quality assurance: The systems and procedures designed and implemented by an organization to ensure that its products and services are of a consistent standard and are being continuously improved. Recognition of prior learning (or RPL): The acknowledgement of a person’s skills and knowledge acquired through previous training, work or life experience, which may be used to grant status or credit in a subject or module. Skills: are the ability to apply knowledge and use the principle of “know how” to perform a specific task and to solve the problem. In the context of the CBE Framework, skills are defined as cognitive (involving the use of logical, intuitive and creative thinking), practical (including physical skill and use of methods, materials, devices and instruments) and social skills (communication and cooperation skills, emotional intelligence and other). Specific competencies: Competencies that are directly related to the tasks of the occupation in the workplace context. They refer to concrete, practical, and focused aspects Traineeship: A system of vocational training combining off-the-job training at an approved training provider with on- the-job training and practical work experience. Traineeships generally take one to two years and are now a part of the New Apprenticeships system. Unit of competency: A component of a competency standard. A unit of competency is a statement of a key function or role in a particular job or occupation. See also element of competency, performance criteria, range of variables.

x | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation FOREWORD The global rapid changes in the labour market tends do call for appropriate training and skills development through outcome-based training approaches. Skills development and employment promotion are central to Rwanda’s transformative Vi sion 2050, aiming to secure high standards of living for all Rwandans. In a bid to transform Rwanda into a knowledge based economy, the National Strategic Transformation 1(NST1) calls socio- economic transformation through TVET skills development. The Rwanda TVET Board (RTB) was established to promote quality education in technical and vocation education and training from level one (1) to five (5) aimed at fast tracking socio-economic development of the country. Designing and distributing curricula, teaching materials, trainer’s guides, methodologies and establish training methods for technical and vocation education and training from level one (1) to five (5); is among other RTB’s responsabilities . The existing curricula were limited and narrowed in terms of acquired skills and knowledge and were not meeting the requirements of the current labour market at both national and regional level. In addition there were. Barriers in vertical mobility and pathways in TVET which resulted in negative TVET perception. Furthermore, the were barriers to admission of TVET graduates of certain programs into higher learning institutions. The TVET modernization process has begun with a clear picture of the programs focusing on sector with the high employment potential like Land Surveying among others. In this respect, Rwanda TVET Board, in collaboration with ENABEL, is honoured to avail the revised curriculum of Land Surveying which serves as the official document and respond to the above mentioned concerns. With the help of the training providers, trainers, parents whose role is central to the success of this curriculum, the trainees will gain appropriate hand on skills which will make a difference not only to their own lives but also to the success of Rwanda’s economy. I wish to sincerely extend my appreciation to the people who contributed towards the development of this document. Eng._ Dip. Paul UMUKUNZI Director General/ RTB
1 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 1. GENERAL INTRODUCTION The curriculum presents a coherent and significant set of competencies to perform the occupation/s of a Building Set out Surveyor, Linear projects Surveyor and Surveyor’s Helper. It is designed with an approach that takes into account the training needs, the work situation, as well as the goals and the means to implement the training. The modules of the curriculum include a description of the expected results of the training. They have a direct influence on the choice of the theoretical and practical learning activities. The competencies are the targets of the training: the acquisition of each is required for certification. The curriculum is the reference to carry out the assessment of learning. Assessment tools of learning are developed based on this document. The curriculum consists of three parts. The first part is of general interest and shows the nature and goals of the program and the key concepts and definitions used in the document. The second part presents the qualification, its level in the qualification framework, its purpose, its rationale and the list of modules it comprises. The third part deals with the training package. It includes the competencies chart, the sequencing of module learning, the description of each module and the course structure. The pages describing the modules are the heart of a curriculum. They present the title of the module, the length of training, the amount of credits, the context in which the competency is performed, the prerequisite competencies, the learning units and the performance criteria. In each module, a course structure is provided. The course structure describes the learning outcomes (knowledge, skills and attitudes) and the learning contents related to each learning unit. In addition, the learning activities and resources for learning are included and where applicable, reference standards are mentioned for indicative contents. Standard reference numbers are indicated throughout the text and the full standards’titles in a separate list under reference section. Finally, the assessment specifications and guidelines are included in each module.
2 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 1.1. Rationale of the Qualification Rwanda’s building and construction industry has rapidly grown in the past couple of years with both government and private sector engaged in the construction of buildings, roads, dams, water treatment plants and new fresh water supply lines, and other infrastructures triggering what is now dubbed as a “construction boom in Rwanda”. The construction industry contributes immensely towards the GDP of the Country mainly through direct income and massive employment opportunities generated from various infrastructure projects, rehabilitation and maintenance. It is estimated that the construction sub-sector of the lar ger industrial sector contributes the highest to the country’s industrial GDP. However, there has been a shortage in skilled surveyors to work in the various formentioned constructions. As such skilled Surveyor worker is the key occupation that need to be addressed to drive the target of the government in construction sector.

Work would be undertaken in various Land surveying and construction entreprises where building setout, pipeline survey, power line survey, terrace, and some road surveying works are carried out. Learners may work with some autonomy or in a team but usually under close supervision. At the end of this qualification, qualified learners will be able to: 1. TRAINING PACKAGE The training package includes the competencies chart, the flowchart, the modules, the course structure, and the assessment guidelines. 3.1 Course structure The course structure describes the learning outcomes for each learning unit. These learning outcomes are the essential skills and knowledge to be acquired. The contents to be covered for each learning outcome are prescriptive. The Learning Activities contain a series of suggestions, usually with several options, that will guide the learner and the trainer. 3.2 Flowchart The flowchart of sequencing of learning is a schematic representation of the order of acquisition of the competencies. It provides an overall planning of the entire training programme and shows the relationship between the modules. This type of planning is to ensure consistency and progression of learning. For each module, the flowchart shows the learning that is already in place, the learning that is to take in parallel or later. The positions defined will have a decisive impact on all subsequent pedagogical choices. The flowchart of the sequence of learning of the modules of the training programme is presented on the following page.

ASSESSMENT GUIDELINES 4.1 Assessment Methodology To assess knowledge, practical, and application skills through a jury system of continuous evaluation that encourages learners to display understanding of the principles in application to set practical tasks and their attendant theory to assess self-learning. There are two types of assessment (Formative Assessment and Summative/Integrated Assessment). Each assessment has its own rule for passing to be declared competent. Formative Assessment This is applied on all types of modules (e.g. Complementary, General and Specific modules) A trainee to be competent for a formative module must have at least 70% A trainee to be eligible to undertake integrated assessment of specific modules must have at least 50% as passing line for general and complementary modules. Each trainee should be competent on all formative assessments to be declared competent on that module All formative assessment should be declared competent before taking the summative/integrated assessment
12 | P a g e Summative Assessment All Summative/Integrated assessment should match with the content of the module in the curriculum. Summative/Integrated Assessment is always in practical, giving it as a theoretical type of assessment is not acceptable. The integrated situation provided in the curriculum is a sample of the assessment to be carried out, the Trainer/Teacher has the role of developing another one referring to the task to be carried out in the integrated situation in accordance to the circumstances inside school, but the integrated situation should stick on the components of a task. During Summative/Integrated assessment, assessor panel members should be three (3). 13 | P a g e GLOSSARY Assessment : A process of gathering and judging evidence in order to decide whether a person has attained a standard of performance. Assessment criteria: Statements which describe performances and place them in context with sufficient precision to allow valid and reliable assessment. Best practice: Management practices and work processes that lead to outstanding or top-class performance and provide examples for others. Competency standard: An industry- determined specification of performance which sets out the skills, knowledge and attitudes required to operate effectively in employment. Competency standards are made up of units of competency, which are themselves made up of elements of competency, together with performance criteria, a range of variables, and an evidence guide. Competency :means the ability to apply knowledge, skills and personal, social and methodological skills in the workplace or during learning, as well as in personal and professional development. This ability or capacity is acquired through leaning, exposure to the tasks and series of training allowing one to perform specific task autonomously. Reason why in the context of the CBE Framework competencies are described as responsibility and independence. Competency-based assessment (or CBA): The gathering and judging of evidence in order to decide whether a person has achieved a standard of competency. Complementary competencies: Set of knowledge, skills and attitudes which are not directly linked to a specific occupation or industry, but which are important for work, education and life in general, such as communication, mathematics, organizational aptitude, and computer literacy, interpersonal and analytical competency. Core modules: Modules leading to competencies’ acquisition that an indus try sector has agreed upon as essential for a person to be accepted as competent at a particular level. All modules may be core, but in many cases competency at a level will involve core modules plus optional or specialization modules. Core competencies are normally those central to work in a particular industry. Credential: Formal certification issued for successful achievement of a defined set of outcomes, e.g. successful completion of a course in recognition of having achieved particular knowledge, skills or competencies; successful completion of an apprenticeship or traineeship. Credit : The acknowledgement that a person has satisfied the requirements of a module. Curriculum: The specifications for a course or subject (module) which describe all the learning experiences a learner undergoes, generally including objectives, content, intended learning outcomes, teaching methodology, recommended or prescribed assessment tasks, assessment exemplars, etc. Evidence guide: The part of a competency standard which provides a guide to the interpretation and assessment of the unit of competency, including the aspects which need to be emphasized in assessment, relationships to other units,
14 | Page Skills for a better destiny and the required evidence of competency. Flexible delivery: A range of approaches to providing education and training, giving learners greater choice of when, where and how they learn. Flexible delivery may involve distance education, mixed-mode delivery, online education, self-paced learning, self-directed learning, etc. Formal education: Also formal training education or training provided in educational institutions such as schools, universities, colleges, etc. or off the job in a workplace, usually involving direction from a teacher or instructor. General competencies: competencies correspond to larger operations that go beyond the tasks, but generally contribute to their implementation. These activities require more fundamental learning and are generally common to several tasks and transferable to many work situations. Generic modules : Modules leading to the attainment of complementary competencies. Informal education: The acquisition of knowledge and skills through experience, reading, social contact, etc. Internship : An opportunity for a learner to integrate career related experience by participating in planned, supervised work. Key competencies: Any of several generic skills or competencies considered essential for people to participate effectively in the workforce. Key competencies apply to work generally, rather than being specific to work in a particular occupation or industry. The following are key areas of competency which were developed into seven key competencies: collecting, analyzing and organizing information; communicating ideas and information; planning and organizing activities; working with others and in teams; using mathematical ideas and techniques; solving problems; and using technology. Knowledge: means the result of the adoption of information through the learning process. Knowledge is a set of facts, principles, theories and practices related to area of work or study. In CBE context lifelong learning knowledge is described as theoretical and / or factual. Learning outcomes : are statements of what learner knows, understands and can perform, based on the completion of the learning process, defined by knowledge, skill and competency. Learning activities: Suggested activities that can be developed during lesson planning and activity preparation. The choice of learning activities must be tailored according to group size, available material resources and communication tools. Learning hours: Amount of hours required to acquire the competency, including the time allocated to evaluation, which is estimated between 5 and 10% of the total learning time of the competency. Learning outcomes: Statements that indicate what learners will know or be able to do as a result of a learning activity. Learning outcomes are usually expressed as knowledge, skills, or attitudes. Learning unit: Any of the basic building blocks of a module, which describes the key activities or the elements of the work covered by the module Module : A unit of training which corresponds to one competency and which can be completed on its own or linked to others. Occupation : The principal business of one’s life.
15 | Page Skills for a better destiny Performance criteria The part of a competency standard specifying the required level of performance in terms of a set of outcomes which need to be achieved in order to be deemed competent. It describes the quality requirements of the result obtained in labor performance. Qualification : means the formal name for the result of a process of assessment and validation, which is obtained when a competent body determines that an individual has achieved learning outcomes to the standards laid down. Quality assurance: The systems and procedures designed and implemented by an organization to ensure that its products and services are of a consistent standard and are being continuously improved. Recognition of prior learning (or RPL): The acknowledgement of a person’s skills and knowledge acquired through previous training, work or life experience, which may be used to grant status or credit in a subject or module. Skills: are the ability to apply knowledge and use the principle of “know how” to perform a specific task and to solve the problem. In the context of the CBE Framework, skills are defined as cognitive (involving the use of logical, intuitive and creative thinking), practical (including physical skill and use of methods, materials, devices and instruments) and social skills (communication and cooperation skills, emotional intelligence and other). Specific competencies: Competencies that are directly related to the tasks of the occupation in the workplace context. They refer to concrete, practical, and focused aspects Traineeship: A system of vocational training combining off-the-job training at an approved training provider with on- the-job training and practical work experience. Traineeships generally take one to two years and are now a part of the New Apprenticeships system. Unit of competency: A component of a competency standard. A unit of competency is a statement of a key function or role in a particular job or occupation. See also element of competency, performance criteria, range of variables.

pages.text: GENAP302 - APPLIED PHYSICS BDCPC301 - Apply general physics Competence GENAP302 RQF Level: 3 Learning Hours 40 Credits: 4 Sector: ALL SECTORS EXCEPT HOSPITALITY AND TOURISM Trade: ALL trades except (Fashion design, Fine and Plastic Arts, Agriculture, Food Processing, Animal Health, Forestry, Leather Technology, Food and Beverages Operations, Front Office and Housekeeping operations, Tourism) Module Type: General Curriculum: GENAP302-TVET - ALL SECTORS EXCEPT HOSPITALITY Copyright: © Rwanda TVET Board, 2022 Issue Date: April 2022 x 1200

1 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This module describes the knowledge, skills, and attitude required to apply concepts of physics. At the end of this module, the trainee will be able to describe basic measurements in physics, analyze motion in one and two dimensions, demonstrate electrostatic phenomena, apply geometric optics and characterize sources of energy in the world. It will help trainee to carry out his/her specialized tasks that are useful in analyzing data, solving real life problems encountered in related fields. Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 50% Practical work: 70% 70% ● Group project and presentation 20% ● Individual project /Work 50% Summative Assessment 50% Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Describe basic measurements in physics 1.1. Physics quantities are clearly derived based on dimension analysis 1.2. Experimental errors are accurately calculated based on the types of errors 1.3. Measuring instruments are properly used based on metric system 2. Describe Motion in 1- Dimension 2.1. Displacement, velocity and acceleration concepts are clearly explained in 1 dimension 2.2. Linear motion concepts are clearly illustrated using corresponding graphs 2.3. Equations of motion are appropriately applied in a straight line under constant acceleration 3. Analyse motion in Two Dimensions 3.1. Scalars, vectors and vector components are clearly described in Cartesian coordinate system 3.2. Displacement, velocity and acceleration concepts are clearly Illustrated in 2 dimensions 3.3. Motion is critically analysed in two dimensions and projectile motion 4. Demonstrate electrostatic phenomena 4.1. Electrostatic charges and their conservation are correctly described in line with laws of static charges on Coulomb’s law and Gauss’s law 4.2. Electrostatic fields are effectively determined based on Coulomb’s law 4.3. Effects of electric field on charged particles are clearly demonstrated based on fundamental laws of static charges

2 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 5. Apply Geometric optics 5.1. Properties of light in homogeneous medium are correctly described based on Fermat’s principle 5.2. Reflection of light on surfaces is effectively applied based on laws of reflection 5.3. Refraction of light in different media is effectively applied based on Snell’s law 6. Characterize sources of energy in the world 6.1. Basic concepts of work, energy and power are properly explained based on the corresponding physical meanings. 6.2. Types of energy are properly identified according to modes of extraction and creation of energy systems in line with sources 6.3. Relative advantages and disadvantages of various energy sources are properly analysed according to the sources 6.4. Linear momentum and kinetic energy in collision are efficiently calculated based on the laws of conservation

3 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Course content Learning outcomes At the end of the module the learner will be able to: 1. Describe basic measurements in physics 2. Describe Motion in 1- Dimension 3. Analyse motion in Two Dimensions 4. Demonstrate electrostatic phenomena 5. Apply Geometric optics 6. 1 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This module describes the knowledge, skills, and attitude required to apply concepts of physics. At the end of this module, the trainee will be able to describe basic measurements in physics, analyze motion in one and two dimensions, demonstrate electrostatic phenomena, apply geometric optics and characterize sources of energy in the world. It will help trainee to carry out his/her specialized tasks that are useful in analyzing data, solving real life problems encountered in related fields. Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 50% Practical work: 70% 70% ● Group project and presentation 20% ● Individual project /Work 50% Summative Assessment 50% Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Describe basic measurements in physics 1.1. Physics quantities are clearly derived based on dimension analysis 1.2. Experimental errors are accurately calculated based on the types of errors 1.3. Measuring instruments are properly used based on metric system 2. Describe Motion in 1- Dimension 2.1. Displacement, velocity and acceleration concepts are clearly explained in 1 dimension 2.2. Linear motion concepts are clearly illustrated using corresponding graphs 2.3. Equations of motion are appropriately applied in a straight line under constant acceleration 3. Analyse motion in Two Dimensions 3.1. Scalars, vectors and vector components are clearly described in Cartesian coordinate system 3.2. Displacement, velocity and acceleration concepts are clearly Illustrated in 2 dimensions 3.3. Motion is critically analysed in two dimensions and projectile motion 4. Demonstrate electrostatic phenomena 4.1. Electrostatic charges and their conservation are correctly described in line with laws of static charges on Coulomb’s law and Gauss’s law 4.2. Electrostatic fields are effectively determined based on Coulomb’s law 4.3. Effects of electric field on charged particles are clearly demonstrated based on fundamental laws of static charges
2 | Page Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 5. Apply Geometric optics 5.1. Properties of light in homogeneous medium are correctly described based on Fermat’s principle 5.2. Reflection of light on surfaces is effectively applied based on laws of reflection 5.3. Refraction of light in different media is effectively applied based on Snell’s law 6. Characterize sources of energy in the world 6.1. Basic concepts of work, energy and power are properly explained based on the corresponding physical meanings. 6.2. Types of energy are properly identified according to modes of extraction and creation of energy systems in line with sources 6.3. Relative advantages and disadvantages of various energy sources are properly analysed according to the sources 6.4. Linear momentum and kinetic energy in collision are efficiently calculated based on the laws of conservation

1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This general module describes the knowledge, skills and attitude required to apply fundamental algebra and trigonometry. The ability to do fundamental algebra and trigonometry is absolutely vital to successfully passing any field. At the end of this module, the trainee of Level Three will be able to solve graphically and algebraically linear or quadratic equations and inequalities. He/she will also be able to apply fundamentals of trigonometry. As Algebra and trigonometry are tools of different fields, this module will be useful to trainee as a means of both measuring and improving their understanding of Mathematics and he/she will be prepared to perform well in any field that requires some knowledge of mathematics especially algebra and trigonometry. The parameter from given equations is properly discussed based on established conditions 1.3. Two simultaneous linear equations are properly solved in accordance with the required steps 1.4. A quadratic equation is effectively solved in accordance with the required steps 2. Apply matrices in solving simultaneous linear equations 2.1. Matrices properties are properly described based on mathematical operations. 2.2. Determinant is correctly computed in line with matrix order. 2.3. Simultaneous linear equations are correctly solved based on Cramer’s method. 3. Apply fundamentals of trigonometry 3.1. Angles are appropriately described based on rotating an initial side, from a fixed point to terminal considered position. 3.2. pages.text: SURVEYING COMMUNICATION LANGUAGE LSVCL301 Apply surveying communication language Competence LSVCL302 RQF Level: 3 Learning Hours 30 Credits: 3 Sector: Construction and Building Services Trade: Land Surveying Module Type: Specific/General/Complementary Curriculum: CBSLSV3001- TVET Certificate 3 in Land Surveying Copyright: © Rwanda TVET Board, 2022 Issue Date: March 2022 1200

1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This module titled Apply surveying communication language was developed for students of RQF Level 3 for the purpose of equipping learners with skills, knowledge and right attitude through the application of surveying hand signals, symbols, abbreviations and surveying terms. Those signals and symbols will help the learners to effectively communicate in the field. Leaning assumed to be in place Safety, Health and environment at workplace; Surveying tools and equipment. Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 100% Practical work: 70% 70% • Group project and presentation 20% • Individual Work 50% Summative Assessment N.A Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Apply surveying hand signals 1.1. Types of hand signals are properly identified according to the information to be conveyed. 1.2. Surveying hand signals are properly described according to their types. 1.3. Surveying hand signals are adequately applied according to the types of information to be conveyed. 2. Apply Surveying symbols 2.1. Types of surveying symbols are properly identified. 2.2. Surveying Symbols are properly described according to their types.

2 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 2.3. Surveying Symbols are adequately applied according to the types of work. 3. Describe surveying terms and abbreviations 3.1. Basic Surveying terms are properly described according to the types of work. 3.2. Basic Surveying abbreviations are properly identified. 3.3. Use of surveying abbreviations is correctly described according to the types of surveying work. Course content Learning outcomes At the end of the module the learner will be able to: 1. Apply Surveying hand signals 2. Apply Surveying symbols 3. Describe surveying terms and abbreviations Identify Surveying hand signals Learning hours: 10 Indicative content ❖ Identification of types of hand signals • Hand signals for numerals • Hand and voice signals ❖ Description of Surveying hand signals • Hand signals for numerals • Hand and voice signals ❖ Application of surveying hand signals • Hand signals for Surveying measurements (Pegging, line ranging, building setting out, pipelines, power transmission line, drainage system, road setting out) • Hand signals for numerals ( eg: Left arm extended diagonally up and shows a simple system for numerals out from, all right, move right or left, give the back sight, give a line or this is a hub, plumb the rod, establish a turning point) • Hand and voice signals Resources required for the learning outcome

3 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Equipment Theodolite, levels, total station. Materials Papers, ink, lead mine, flip chart, notebook, pens, and pencils. Tools Flags, pegs, ranging rods, staff reading, ink pens, lead mine pens. Facilitation techniques • Demonstration and simulation • Individual and group work • Practical exercise • Trainer guided • Group discussion Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Oral assessment • Practical assessment Apply Surveying symbols Learning hours: 10 Indicative content ❖ Identification of types of surveying symbols • Map symbols • Standard symbols • Topographic symbols • Convention symbols ❖ Description of surveying symbols • Map symbols • Standard symbols • Topographic map symbols (cultural symbols, natural features symbols, constructed features, hydrographical features, water features) • Convention symbol • Map legend • Surveyors symbols • Mineral survey symbols Application of surveying symbols

4 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation • Marsh or swarm, house, embankment, single line railway, lake or pond, road, railway bridge, river and fence. • Demonstration of symbols on maps and plans • Locate and differentiate symbols on surveying field Resources required for the indicative content Equipment GPS receiver, DGNSS receiver, level, ODM, DDM, EDM. Materials Papers spray paint, nails, pegs. Tools Plans, maps, pencils, pens, marker pens, pins, flags, monuments, beacons, claw hammers, machete, pick axe, plumb bob, tape measures. Facilitation techniques • Demonstration and simulation • Individual and group work • Practical exercise • Trainer guided • Group discussion Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Oral presentation • Performance assessment Describe basic surveying terms and abbreviations Learning hours: 10 Indicative content ❖ Description of basic surveying terms • Topographic surveying terms (mapping, contour lines, traversing, etc.) • Cadastral surveying terms (land subdivision, registration, cadastre, etc.) • Levelling terms (Mean sea level, datum, benchmark, reduced level, etc.) • Angular measurements terms (bearing, zenith, azimuth, etc.) • Linear measurements terms (direct and indirect, slope, height, etc.) ❖ Identification of basic surveying abbreviations • Linear measurements abbreviations (EDM, PK, etc.) • Levelling surveying abbreviations (BM, RL, CP, etc.)

5 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation • Angular measurements abbreviations (WCB, RB, etc.) • Topographic surveying abbreviations (TBM, PK, HI, etc.) ❖ Application domain of basic surveying abbreviations • Road construction surveying • Topographic surveying • Angular measurements • Levelling surveying • Linear measurements • Cadastral surveying • Cartography • Construction surveying • Mining surveying Resources required for the indicative content Equipment GPS, DGPS, total station, level, theodolite, EDM. Materials Papers, spray paint, nails, pegs. Tools Plans, maps, pencils, pens, marker pens, pins, flags, monuments, beacons, claw hammers, machete, pick axe, plumb bob, tape measures. Facilitation techniques • Individual and group work • Trainer guided • Group discussion Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Oral assessment

6 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation References: 1. Ghasemi, A and Sousa,E(2005). "Collaborative Spectrum Sensing for Opportunistic Access in Fading Environments", in Proc. of IEEE International Symposium on New Frontiers in Dyna Spectrum Access Networks (DySPAN 2005), pp. 131-136 2. IEEE Communications Magazine (April 2008). Standardization efforts. IEEE Communications.Institute of Technology. 3. ITU Radio Regulations. (2008) International Telecommunication Union. Genève Magazine, April 2008, pp. 72- 78 4. MATLAB. (2014). International Journal of Next Generation Networks (IJNGN) Vol.6, No.2, June 5. Mitola and Maguire. (2000). Applied Computational Electromagnetics. Hawaii 6. Mitola,J (2000). "Cognitive Radio: An Integrated Agent Architecture for Software Defined Radio", PhD thesis, KTH Royal Institute of Technology. Stockholm: KTH Royal 7. Samuel, C. (2012). pages.text: HYGIENE AND SAFETY PRECAUTIONS MEASURES Apply hygiene and safety precautions measures Competence L SVHS302 RQF Level: 3 Learning Hours 30 Credits: 3 Sector: Construction and Building Services Trade: Land Surveying Module Type: Specific Curriculum: CBSLSV3001- TVET Certificate 3 in Land Surveying Copyright: © Rwanda TVET Board, 2022 Issue Date: May 2022 1200

1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This module is designed for a student pursuing a level 3 TVET certificate in Land Surveying. It describes the skills, knowledge, and right attitudes required to apply hygiene and safety precautions measures at surveying the workplace. At the end of this module, the students will be able to select surveying personal protective equipment, identify and handle hazards and emergencies at the surveying workplace, and to maintain surveying equipment . Leaning assumed to be in place N/A Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 100% Practical work: 70% 70% • Group project and presentation 20% • Individual project /Work 20% Summative assessment N.A. Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Select surveying personal 1.1. Types of surveying personal protective equipment are properly identified according to the weather condition, type of work,

2 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation protective equipment and terrain characteristics . 1.2. Surveying personal protective equipment is appropriately used according to the weather condition, type of work, and terrain characteristics. 1.3. Personal protective equipment is properly cared according to their maintenance and storage system. 2. Identify and handle Hazards and emergencies at surveying the Workplace 2.1. Hazards and emergencies are properly identified at surveying workplace. 2.2. Surveying hazards and emergencies are appropriately handled at the workplace. 2.3. Hazards and emergencies are adequately evaluated according to their types. 3. Maintain surveying equipment 3.1. Hygiene of surveying equipment is appropriately done according to the types of equipment and manufacturer’s catalogue 3.2. Surveying equipment is appropriately transported according to the type of equipment 3.3. Surveying equipment is adequately stored according to manufacturer ’s catalogue Course content Learning outcomes At the end of the module the learner will be able to: 1. Select surveying personal protective equipment 2. Identify and handle hazards and emergencies in surveying the workplace 3. Maintain surveying instruments

3 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Learning outcome 1: Select surveying personal protective equipment Learning hours: 7 Indicative content  Types of surveying personal protective equipment (Refer to RS ISO 20347, RS ISO 13688, ISO 3873, ISO 21420, ISO 17420-1) • Head protection, foot protection, hands protection, body protection, eye protection, ear protection, respiratory protection, etc.  The use of surveying personal protective equipment (PPE) • Helmet, safety shoes, safety boots, gloves, overalls, reflector jacket, safety goggles, safety glasses, earplugs, earmuff, mask, etc.  Maintenance and storage of surveying personal protective equipment • Maintenance of PPE ( cleaning, examination, replacement, repair, and testing ) • Storage of PPE ( Hanging, Laying, clothing, container/box ) Resources required for the learning outcome Equipment High visibility jackets, safety boots &knee pads, gloves, glasses &goggles, respiratory masks, earplugs & earmuff, and safety helmets, whiteboard, projector, computer Materials Water , pens, notebooks, marker pen, soap, flipcharts, etc. Tools Surveyor’s bags , brushes, sponge , etc…. Facilitation techniques • Group work • Practical exercise • Discussion • Brainstorming • Trainer guided Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Oral assessment

4 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Learning outcome 2: Identify Hazards and emergencies at surveying Workplace Learning hours: 9 Indicative content  Identify Hazards and emergencies at surveying the Workplace (Refer to ISO 18400-103) • Types of hazards (Safety hazards, Chemical hazards, Biological hazards). • Types of emergencies (Natural emergencies, Work-related emergencies). • Comparison between hazard and emergency.  Handling surveying hazards and emergencies at the workplace • Method of handling surveying hazards at the workplace ( Use protective clothing and equipment, Improve work policies and procedures). • Method of handling surveying emergencies at the workplace ( Determine the nature of the emergency, remain calm , assess the immediate threat , etc. ).  Evaluation of Hazards and emergencies • Steps/procedures to evaluate types of hazards at surveying workplace. • Steps/procedures to evaluate types of emergences at surveying workplace. Resources required for the indicative content Equipment Measuring devices, fire extinguishers, first aid kits, whiteboard, flipcharts stand, projector, computer. Materials Chalk/paint, pens, notebooks, marker pen, flipcharts. Tools Safety cones, videos, stories and pictures Facilitation techniques • Demonstration and simulation • Individual and group work • Practical exercise • Case study • Trainer guided • Group discussion Formative assessment • Written assessment

5 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation methods • Oral assessment Learning outcome 3: Maintain surveying equipment Learning hours: 14 Indicative content  Hygiene of surveying equipment (Refer to ISO 9849, ISO 12510) • Cleaning method, • Lubrication methods  Transportation of surveying equipment • O perator’s Manual , • Routine Care of Equipment  Storage of surveying equipment • Storeroom • Casing and uncasing Resources required for the indicative content Equipment Storeroom, vehicle, computer, dumpy level, theodolite, total station, GPS, whiteboard, computer, and projector. Materials Water, oil, brushes, marker pen, pieces of chalk, notebook. Tools Toolbox, markers, wheelbarrow Facilitation techniques • Demonstration and simulation • Individual and group work • Practical exercise • Trainer guided • Group discussion Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Oral assessment • Performance assessment

1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This module titled leveling surveys application was developed for students of RQF Level 3 land surveying for the purpose of equipping them with the skills, knowledge, and attitudes required to apply leveling techniques in projects related to measuring elevations. At the end of this module, the learner will be able to describe methods of leveling, perform instrument adjustments, and apply leveling techniques to determine elevations or differences in elevations of points and/or to establish points at various given elevations. Leaning assumed to be in place Safety, Health and environment at workplace; Surveying tools and equipment; Surveying communication language; Linear distance measurement; Construction drawings interpretation; Building setting out; Angular measurements. Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 50% Practical work: 70% 70% • Group project and presentation 20% • Individual project /Work 50% Summative Assessment 50% Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Describe methods of levelling 1.1. Levelling terms are properly described. 1.2. Direct Levelling methods are properly described according to their use. 1.3. Indirect Levelling methods are properly described according to their use. 2. Perform levelling 2.1. Levelling instruments are properly identified according to

2 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation instrument adjustments their types . 2.2. Parts of levelling instruments are well described according to the types of instruments. 2.3. The levels are temporally adjusted according to their types. 2.4. The levels are permanently adjusted according to their axes. 3. Apply levelling methods to real case projects 3.1. Levels are properly taken and booked according to the types of readings. 3.2. Reduced levels (RLs) are correctly calculated according to the methods of booking. 3.3. Profile levelling is properly applied according to their types. 3.4. Levelling is properly applied according to the earthwork calculations. 3.5. Levelling is properly applied according to the contour map generation. 3.6. Levelling errors are correctly adjusted according to their Sources. Leaning assumed to be in place Safety, Health and environment at workplace; Surveying tools and equipment; Surveying communication language. 1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This core module describes the skills, knowledge and attitude required to perform angles measurements. At the end of this module, student should be able to describe surveying instruments, tools and materials used in angular measurement; perform surveying instruments set up, and perform field angles measuring. Leaning assumed to be in place Safety, Health and environment at workplace; Surveying tools and equipment; Surveying communication language; Linear distance measurement; Construction drawings interpretation; Building setting out. Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 50% Practical work: 70% 70% • Group project and presentation 20% • Individual project /Work 50% Summative Assessment 50% Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Describe Surveying Instruments, tools and materials in angles measurements 1.1 Surveying instruments, tools, and materials used in angles measurements are properly identified according to their use. 1.2 Surveying instruments and tools are appropriately classified according to their functions and construction design. 1.3 Angular measurement units are adequately identified in accordance with their unit types. 2. Perform Surveying 2.1 Surveying instruments and tools are properly selected according to the task requirements.

2 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Instruments set up 2.2 Surveying instruments are correctly set up according to their instructional manual. 2.3 Surveying instruments are properly adjusted according to the their types. 3. Perform field angles measurements 3.1. Types of angles are properly determined according to their applications. 3.2. Methods of measuring angles are properly selected in accordance with their accuracies. 3.3. Angles are accurately measured in traverse according to the conventional procedures. 3.4. Errors of measured angles are accurately adjusted according to their types. Course content Learning outcomes At the end of the module the learner will be able to: 1. Describe surveying instruments, tools, and materials in angles measurements 2. Perform Surveying instruments set up 3. Perform field angles measurements Learning outcome 1: Describe Surveying Instruments, Tools and Materials in angles measurements Learning hours: 12 Indicative content  Surveying instruments; tools and materials used in angles measurements (Refer to ISO 8322-4, ISO 17123-2, IS0 1141) • Surveying instruments ( compass, theodolite, tacheometer, levels, etc. ) • Surveying tools ( tripod, ranging rods, plumb bob, claw hammer, club hammer, panga, hand saw, etc.) • Materials ( building lines, pegs, paper, pen, nails, theodolite batteries, e tc… )  Classification of surveying instruments used in angles measurements

3 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation • Classification of Theodolites ✓ Based on technology used (repeating theodolites, directional theodolites, electrical digital theodolites, total station) ✓ Based on movement of telescope about the horizontal axis in a vertical plane (Transit theodolites, Non transit theodolites) ✓ Based on arrangement to measure the angles (vernier theodolites, micrometer theodolites/precise optical theodolites, electronic or digital theodolites) • Classification/Types of Compass (Prismatic Compass, Surveyor’s Compass, etc….)  Angular measurement units • Angular measurement units system (sexagesmal system, centesimal system, radian system) • Converting the angular measurement units system (sexagesmal to centesimal system, centesimal to sexagesmal system, sexagesmal to radian system, radian to sexagesmal system, centesimal to radian system, radian to centesimal system) Resources required for the learning outcome Equipment Theodolite , compass , tacheometer , automatic level , dumpy level, whiteboard, projector , computer. pages.text: BDCPC301 - Prepare surveying project quantities and cost estimates Competence LSVQC302 RQF Level: 3 Learning Hours 40 Credits: 4 Sector: Construction and Building Services Trade: Land surveying Module Type: Specific Curriculum: CBSLSV3001 - TVET Certificate 3 in Land surveying Copyright: © Rwanda TVET Board, 2022 Issue Date: May 2022 x 1200

1 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Purpose statement This module is designed for students pursuing level 3 TVET certificate in land surveying. It describes the skills, knowledge, and attitude required to estimate quantity and cost of surveying projects. At the end of this module, the student will be able to estimate quantities, analyze costs and produce an abstract of cost for a surveying project. Leaning assumed to be in place Safety, Health and environment at workplace; Surveying tools and equipment; Surveying communication language; Linear distance measurement; Construction drawings interpretation; Building setting out; Angular measurements. Delivery modality Training delivery 100% Assessment Total 100% Theoretical content 30% Formative assessment 30% 50% Practical work: 70% 70% • Group project and presentation 20% • Individual project /Work 50% Summative Assessment 50% Elements of Competency and Performance Criteria Elements of competency Performance criteria 1. Estimate quantities for surveying projects 1.1. Items of surveying work are correctly identified with respect to the surveying project. 1.2. Items are correctly described with respect to the surveying project 1.3. Quantities are accurately calculated based on the surveying project.

2 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation 2. Analyse costs for surveying projects 2.1. Direct cost is accurately calculated according to the surveying project. 2.2. Indirect cost is accurately calculated in accordance with the surveying project. 2.3. Contingency cost is properly analyzed and calculated according to the given surveying project. 3. Produce bills of quantities and costs 3.1. Bill of quantities is correctly elaborated according to the methods of measurement. 3.2. Unit rates are properly analyzed with respect to the surveying project. 3.3. Abstract of costs is correctly elaborated based on the method of measurement. Course content Learning outcomes At the end of the module the learner will be able to: 1. Estimate quantities for surveying project 2. Analyse costs for surveying project 3. Elaborate bills of quantities and costs Learning outcome 1: Quantities estimation for surveying project Learning hours: 13 Indicative content  Surveying project items (Refer to ISO 230-6) • Materials, tools, instruments, equipment, labour  Description of items • Specification of items • Unit of measurement of each item  Calculation of quantities for items • Rough methods of quantities estimation • Detailed methods of quantities estimation Resources required for the learning outcome

3 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Equipment Computer, white/blackboard, projector. Materials Marker pen, pieces of chalk, notebooks, pieces paper. Tools Calculator, pens, markers, pencils Facilitation techniques • Group discussion • Group work • Trainer guided • Practical works Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Performing assessment • Product based assessment Learning outcome 2: Costs analysis surveying project for Learning hours: 13 Indicative content  Calculation of direct costs • Determination of costs of material, labor, equipment, tools, and instrument.  Calculation of indirect costs • Transport, profit, taxes, depreciation, overhead, etc.  Calculation of contingency costs • Types of contingency costs • Analysis and calculation of contingency costs Resources required for the indicative content Equipment Computer, white/blackboard, projector. Materials Pieces of chalk, notebooks, pieces of paper. Tools Calculator, pens, pencils, markers. Facilitation techniques • Individual and group work • Practical exercise • Trainer guided • Group discussion Formative assessment • Written assessment • Performing assessment

4 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation methods • Product based assessment Learning outcome 3: Produce bills of quantities and costs Learning hours: 14 Indicative content  Bill of quantities elaboration • Elements of the bill of quantities • Format of the bill of quantities  Unit rates analysis • Types of unit rates • Factors affecting unit rates. • Calculation of unit rates.  Abstract of costs elaboration • Format of abstract of cost • Content of abstract of cost and calculation of total cost Resources required for the indicative content Equipment Computer, white/blackboard, projector. Materials Marker pen, pieces of chalk, notebooks, pieces of paper. Tools abstract of cost sheet, calculator, pens, pencils Facilitation techniques • Individual and group work • Trainer guided • Group discussion • Practical works Formative assessment methods • Written assessment • Performing assessment • Product based assessment

5 | P a g e Employable Skills for Sustainable Job Creation Integrated/Summative assessment (For specific module) Integrated situation AMITH TVET School situated in the Kayonza district wants to construct a football playground. The existing terrain is not levelled. The proposed playground must be 100m long and 50m wide. The surveying task to be performed consists of setting the playground boundaries and leveling the terrain. During levelling the interval between pegs must be 10m. The task will be completed using dumpy level, tape measures, hammer, marker pen, strings, and nails. As a land surveyor, you are hired to conduct surveying-related works. ✓ Estimate quantities for all items related to surveying works (Tools, materials, instruments, equipment, and labour). ✓ Estimate the cost for each item related to surveying works. ✓ Prepare a bill of quantity and cost estimation related to the surveying works to be done. The maximum time to complete the given task is 3 hours.
